vignette:
# Marcus

Marcus is a 54-year-old civil servant who has spent the better part of three decades working in local government planning. He is methodical by nature, the kind of man who takes satisfaction in orderly files and processes that follow predictable rules. He sits in the therapy room with his hands folded in his lap, and there is something careful about the way he occupies space — as though he has learned to take up as little of it as possible.

For six years, Marcus was in a relationship with a woman he describes, with some difficulty, as "magnetic." He met her when he was in his mid-forties, recently divorced, and, as he puts it, "probably lonelier than I admitted to myself." The relationship began warmly, but within the first year the violence started. It was not constant — there were long stretches of calm that made him doubt his own memory of what had happened. She would strike him across the face during arguments, throw objects, once fractured two of his ribs when she pushed him into the edge of a kitchen counter. He did not call the police. He tells himself now that he was ashamed, that no one would have believed him, that he kept thinking things would return to how they had been at the beginning.

He ended the relationship two years ago after she broke his nose during what had begun as a disagreement about dinner plans. Something shifted in him that night — not rage, he says, but a cold, exhausted clarity. He left and did not go back.

What Marcus did not anticipate was that leaving would not mean safety. He lives now with a partner he describes as genuinely kind, and he recognises this intellectually, but his nervous system has not caught up with that knowledge. When she raises her voice even slightly — in laughter, in surprise, in ordinary frustration — Marcus feels his body lock. His heart hammers. He finds himself scanning her hands, watching for the particular tension in her shoulders that used to precede an attack. He has startled her more than once by flinching when she reached past him for something on a shelf.

Sleep is fractured and unreliable. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, his chest tight, sometimes with the physical sensation of a blow that hasn't landed. He has stopped telling his partner about the nightmares because he sees the worry on her face and cannot bear to be the cause of it. At work, he manages. The structure of the office, the predictability of planning applications and committee meetings, gives him something to organise himself around. But his concentration has narrowed. He re-reads the same paragraph four or five times. Colleagues have commented, gently, that he seems elsewhere.

He avoids anything that carries the texture of that period. He has not watched television programmes involving domestic arguments. He changed his route to work so he no longer passes the street where she lived. When a younger male colleague recently confided that he was having relationship difficulties, Marcus found himself unable to engage — he made an excuse and retreated to his office, where he sat for twenty minutes doing nothing at all.

What troubles Marcus most, and what he mentions with visible discomfort, is the shame that has not lifted. He is a grown man, he says. He managed a department of twelve people. He cannot reconcile who he believed himself to be with what he allowed to happen — though he uses the word "allowed" and then immediately catches himself, as if he knows it is wrong but cannot quite release it. He describes feeling hollowed out, like something essential was taken from him that he has not yet found a way to reclaim. He wants to be present for his current partner. He wants to sleep through the night. He wants, most simply, to stop flinching at the sound of someone else's happiness.
